description_full: Abercrombie & Fitch Co., through its subsidiaries, operates as an omnichannel retailer in the Americas, Europe, the Middle East, Africa, and the Asia-Pacific. It offers an assortment of apparel, personal care products, and accessories for men, women, and kids under the Abercrombie & Fitch, abercrombie kids, Your Personal Best, Hollister, and Gilly Hicks brands. The company sells products through its stores, various wholesale, franchise, and licensing arrangements, as well as e-commerce platforms. Abercrombie & Fitch Co. was founded in 1892 and is headquartered in New Albany, Ohio.
ceo_bio: Ms. Fran  Horowitz | CEO & Director | Age 61 | Compensation: $2.8M (FY2025)
culture_narrative: Employs approximately 6K people. Revenue per employee of $798K ranks in the top quartile among Consumer Cyclical peers. Each employee generates $57K of free cash flow annually. Stock-based compensation of $6K per employee reflects an ownership culture. CEO compensation is 4× revenue per employee (modest relative to workforce productivity). Governance score flags low compensation governance risk (1/10).
financial_summary: Abercrombie & Fitch Company is a mid-cap consumer cyclical business with a $6.3B market cap on $5.3B of annual revenue.
The top line has compounded at +13% over the past three years and +4% annually across the full decade, the kind of sustained demand persistence that marks a compounder.
Returns on capital run at 94% against a 10% cost of capital — a 83-point spread that is the clearest signature of an economic moat. Gross margins of 61% confirm genuine pricing power.

The business throws off $378M in free cash flow — roughly 7 cents on every revenue dollar, which is the owner-earnings figure that actually belongs to shareholders, and cash conversion sits at 1.22× so those profits are backed by real cash.
On the balance sheet, the balance sheet carries net cash, which is the gold standard: the business never has to make desperate decisions in a bad year, and interest coverage of 40× is fortress-like.

Management returns a meaningful 7.1% of market cap to owners through dividends and buybacks, a strong signal of disciplined capital allocation, and insiders hold 2.2% of the shares, and within its sector the business captures 1.7× its fair share of profits, a structural advantage visible in the numbers.

E-commerce margin compression and tariff exposure — digital competition erodes pricing power while trade policy reshuffles supply-chain cost structures overnight.
Brand relevance decay — shifting consumer preferences and social-media-driven trends can strand inventory and invalidate positioning faster than product cycles can adapt.

sect: Its 13% operating margin runs 6pp above the Consumer Cyclical median (7%), a real cost or pricing edge over peers.
It captures 1.67x its revenue share in sector profits, taking a disproportionate slice of the profit pool.
The sector is fragmented and competitive (HHI 0.03 across 377 companies in the universe; the top four hold 26% of revenue), so pricing power is hard to come by.
mkt: The shares are in a strong uptrend, up 111% over the past year excluding the latest month.
The price sits mid-way through its 52-week range, 13% below the high.
With annualised volatility of 73% and a beta of 1.14, it moves roughly with the market.
Liquidity is deep, with about $176.4M traded a day.
In past sell-offs it fell 56% in the 2020 crash, 65% in the 2022 bear market and 83% in 2008.
val: The stock trades 33% below its DCF fair value of $223, a meaningful margin of safety.
The fair-value models disagree (dispersion 25%), and the Monte Carlo range runs $159 to $320 (P10-P90), so treat the estimate as noisy.
On multiples it looks cheap against Consumer Cyclical peers: P/E 12.9 vs 18.8 and EV/EBITDA 7.7 vs 10.7 (sector median).
Against its own history it is dear: the EBIT multiple sits 7% above its 10-year median.
Earnings yields are attractive: an FCF yield of 6.0% (above the risk-free rate) and an EBIT/EV of 9.9% (vs the 8% bar).
The 11 covering analysts target $170 on average, 14% above the price.
prof: ROIC of 94% clears the cost of capital of 10.2% by 83pp, the mark of a value creator; returns have swung a lot from year to year (CV 1.42).
It runs a 61% gross margin and converts 7% of revenue into free cash flow.
Earnings quality looks solid: cash conversion of 1.22x.
ROE of 36% comes mostly from margins and asset turnover rather than leverage (2.5x equity multiplier).
Operating margin is running 7pp above its own historical average, a peak-margin risk if conditions normalise.
It spends 0.7% of revenue on stock compensation.
hlth: The company holds more cash than debt.
growth: Revenue has compounded at 12.5% over 3 years, 11.0% over 5 years and 4.1% over 10 years.
At current returns, reinvesting 17% of profits supports about 15.7% a year of fundamental growth, enough to sustain growth.
Free cash flow has compounded 4.5% a year over five years, short of the 5% durability bar.
Capex runs 1.6x depreciation (4.6% of sales), so it is building capacity for future growth.
Its Rule of 40 score is 17, below the 40 that marks a healthy growth business.
It has beaten earnings estimates by 35.0% on average.
own: Insiders own a modest 2.2%, and reported institutional holdings exceed 100% of shares (a sign of heavy share lending).
Insiders have only sold over the past year (8 sales, net $6.2M sold).
It returns 7.1% a year to shareholders (7.1% in buybacks).
The share count has shrunk 5.6% a year over five years, steadily raising each holder's stake.
Short interest is elevated at 15.4% of the float, 4.0 days to cover.
people: With about 6,600 employees, each generates about $798K of revenue, 2.1x the Consumer Cyclical median, and revenue has grown 2.8% a year across its filed history.
That works out to $57K of free cash flow per employee.
CEO pay is $2.8M (4x revenue per employee), and compensation governance scores well (1/10, lower is better).
